entry: Fifth-generation home video game console made by Sega. Released in Japan on November 22, 1994, the Saturn succeeded the [[Sega Genesis|Genesis]] and had a dual-CPU architecture. Its games used CD-ROM discs, including several ports of arcade games. The Saturn was initially successful in Japan but not in the United States, where a surprise May 1995 launch hindered it. After the [[Nintendo 64]] debuted in late 1996, its U.S. market share fell rapidly, and it was discontinued there in 1998. Lifetime sales were 9.26 million units, most in Japan.

American television sitcom created by [[Larry David]] and [[Jerry Seinfeld]]. It aired on [[NBC]] from July 5, 1989, to May 14, 1998, over nine seasons and 180 episodes. Jerry Seinfeld plays a fictionalized version of himself, and the show follows his life with friends in an apartment in [[Manhattan]], New York City. Often described as "a show about nothing," it focuses on the minutiae of daily life. Stand-up comedy segments by Seinfeld appear in all episodes of the first seven seasons. The series led the Nielsen ratings in seasons 6 and 9, and quotations from its episodes became catchphrases.

Scales for the overall strength, or size, of an [[Earthquake|earthquake]]. They are distinct from seismic intensity scales, which rate the severity of ground shaking at a given location. Magnitude is usually determined from seismic waves recorded on a seismogram, using measures such as timing, orientation, [[Amplitude|amplitude]], frequency or duration. Magnitude is approximately related to the released seismic energy. Different scales exist because earthquakes differ, the available information differs, and magnitudes serve different purposes.

Scientific study of [[Earthquake|earthquakes]] and the propagation of elastic waves through planets. The field also covers the environmental effects of earthquakes, such as [[Tsunami|tsunamis]], and seismic sources including volcanoes and [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]]. Paleoseismology uses [[Geology|geology]] to infer information about past earthquakes, and a seismogram records Earth's motion over time. Scholarly interest in earthquakes dates to antiquity; in 132 CE [[Zhang Heng]] of China's Han dynasty designed the first known seismoscope. In 1906 Richard Dixon Oldham found the first clear evidence that Earth has a central core. In 1910 Harry Fielding Reid proposed the "elastic rebound theory," which remains the foundation for modern tectonic studies.

Fourth monarch of the [[Joseon]] state of Korea (r. 1418–1450). He is particularly remembered for creating [[Hangul]], the native alphabet of the [[Korean language]]. His reign saw major developments in science, technology, medicine, agriculture and the arts; he oversaw the first native Korean calendar, Ch'ilchŏngsan, and the 365-volume medical text Ŭibangyuch'wi. In 1419 he launched the successful Ōei Invasion against Tsushima Island, which was followed by decades of peace and trade between Korea and Japan. He expanded Korea's northern borders to roughly their current extent and maintained positive relations with the Ming while asserting Korean autonomy. He expanded Confucian influence at the expense of Buddhism, though he was privately Buddhist. Sejong City in South Korea bears his name.

Process of choosing which animals or plants reproduce in order to develop particular traits. Also called artificial selection, it is often combined with [[Inbreeding|inbreeding]], linebreeding and outcrossing. Domesticated animals are known as breeds, and domesticated plants as varieties or cultivars. [[Charles Darwin]] used artificial selection as an analogy for [[Natural selection|natural selection]] in *On the Origin of Species* (1859). Selective breeding has been practiced since prehistory: wheat, rice and [[Dog|dogs]] differed from their wild ancestors for millennia, and [[Maize|maize]] was bred from teosinte in [[Mesoamerica]]. Robert Bakewell established it as a scientific practice during Britain's Agricultural Revolution in the 18th century. It is now common in agriculture and experimental biology.

Class of antidepressant drugs that block the reuptake of [[Serotonin|serotonin]] through its transporter in the brain. They are mainly used to treat [[Major depressive disorder]] and anxiety disorders, and are also prescribed for eating disorders and chronic pain. Marketed examples include citalopram, escitalopram, [[Fluoxetine|fluoxetine]], fluvoxamine, paroxetine and [[Sertraline|sertraline]]. SSRIs are the most widely prescribed antidepressants in many countries. A 2018 meta-analysis of 21 antidepressants found all were more effective than placebo for adults with major depressive disorder, but the certainty of evidence was rated moderate to very low.

American singer-songwriter and fashion designer, known as the "Queen of Tejano Music." Her popularity grew after she won the Tejano Music Award for Female Vocalist of the Year in 1987, a title she won nine consecutive times. Her album *Entre a Mi Mundo* (1992) peaked at number one on the Billboard Regional Mexican Albums chart for eight consecutive months. *Live!* (1993) won Best Mexican/American Album at the 1994 [[Grammy Awards]]. She was shot and killed in 1995 by Yolanda Saldívar, a friend and former boutique manager. Her posthumous album *Dreaming of You* debuted atop the Billboard 200. A 1997 film about her starred [[Jennifer Lopez]].

American actress, singer and entrepreneur. She became a teen idol as Alex Russo in the [[Disney Channel]] sitcom *Wizards of Waverly Place*, and formed the band Selena Gomez & the Scene. Her album *Revival* (2015) reached the top five of the US Billboard Hot 100 with singles including "Good for You." *Rare* (2020) produced the number-one single "Lose You to Love Me." She has starred in films including *Spring Breakers* (2012) and *Emilia Pérez* (2024), and has played a lead role in *Only Murders in the Building* since 2021. A [[UNICEF]] Goodwill Ambassador, she founded the cosmetics company Rare Beauty.

Chemical element with symbol Se and atomic number 34. Discovered in 1817 by [[Jöns Jacob Berzelius]], who noted its similarity to the previously discovered [[Tellurium|tellurium]], selenium takes its name from the Greek word for "moon." It is found in metal sulfide ores, where it substitutes for [[Sulfur|sulfur]], and is produced commercially as a byproduct of refining them. Its chief uses are in glassmaking and pigments, and it is a [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] used in photocells. Trace amounts are necessary for cellular function in many animals, including humans, but both elemental selenium and its salts are toxic in small doses, causing selenosis. Selenium is a component of the antioxidant enzymes glutathione peroxidase and thioredoxin reductase.

Hellenistic Greek state in West Asia (312–63 BC). It was founded by the Macedonian general [[Seleucus I Nicator|Seleucus I]] after the division of the empire of [[Alexander the Great]]. At its height it covered Anatolia, Persia, the Levant, Mesopotamia and parts of Central Asia. It was a center of Hellenistic culture, and an urban Greek elite formed its dominant political class. Its western territories were repeatedly contested with [[Egypt|Ptolemaic Egypt]]. After defeat by the [[Roman Republic]] at the Battle of Magnesia, the Seleucids lost territory west of the Taurus Mountains in southern Anatolia. The Seleucid rump state in Syria was conquered by [[Tigranes the Great]] of Armenia in 83 BC and overthrown by the Roman general [[Pompey]] in 63 BC.

Macedonian general and founder of the [[Seleucid Empire]]. A commander under [[Alexander the Great]], Seleucus was appointed satrap of Babylon in 321 BC, but he was forced to flee when the Wars of the Diadochi resumed. He returned to Babylon in 312 BC with Ptolemy's support and expanded his dominions into Persia and Media. A treaty with [[Chandragupta Maurya]] ended the Seleucid–Mauryan War, transferring the eastern satrapies to the [[Maurya Empire]] and bringing Seleucus 500 [[War elephant|war elephants]]. He defeated Lysimachus at Corupedium in 281 BC, but was assassinated by Ptolemy Ceraunus upon arriving in Thrace. He founded [[Antioch]] and Seleucia on the [[Tigris]], among other cities.

Principle of international law that a people has the right to form its own political entity. The principle does not specify how the decision is made or what the outcome should be, whether independence, federation or autonomy, and no right to secession is recognized under international law. The concept emerged with 19th-century nationalism. [[Woodrow Wilson]] and others proclaimed a general principle of self-determination during and after [[World War I]], and it was included in the 1941 Atlantic Charter. It was recognized as an international legal right when it was listed in the [[United Nations]] Charter. Implementing it is difficult because there are multiple interpretations of what constitutes a people. As World Court judge Ivor Jennings put it, "the people cannot decide until somebody decides who are the people."

Confidence in one's own worth, abilities or morals. It encompasses beliefs about oneself, such as "I am worthy," as well as emotional states such as triumph, pride and [[Shame|shame]]. Psychologists usually regard it as an enduring personality trait, although short-term variations also exist. High self-esteem is associated with academic achievement, relationship satisfaction, happiness and lower rates of criminal behavior, while low self-esteem has been linked to anxiety, [[Loneliness|loneliness]] and vulnerability to substance abuse. The concept was first expressed by the Scottish Enlightenment thinker [[David Hume]] in the 18th century, and [[William James]] identified it as a distinct psychological construct. In the mid-1960s Morris Rosenberg defined self-esteem as a feeling of self-worth and developed the Rosenberg self-esteem scale, the most widely used such scale in the social sciences. Self-esteem typically declines from ages 4–8 and peaks around ages 60–70.

Intentional injury to one's own body, usually without suicidal intent. Common methods include cutting, scratching, hitting or burning. Although non-suicidal by definition, it can be life-threatening: people who self-harm are more likely to die by [[Suicide|suicide]], and 40–60% of people who die by suicide have previously self-harmed. The desire to self-harm is a common symptom of some [[Personality disorder|personality disorders]]. It often serves as a coping mechanism for intense feelings such as anxiety, depression or emotional numbness, and it is associated with a history of trauma. It tends to begin in [[Adolescence|adolescence]]. Treatments address underlying causes or the behavior itself.

[[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] sultan (r. 1789–1807) who sought to modernize the state through military, administrative and educational reforms. He created the Nizam-i Cedid in 1797, a European-style army trained and equipped along modern lines, and established permanent embassies in major European capitals. His reign was marked by wars against Austria, Russia and Revolutionary [[France]], including [[Napoleon]]'s invasion of Egypt. Regarded as an enlightened ruler, he patronized music, poetry and the arts, and he wrote poems. He was deposed by the [[Janissary|Janissaries]], who placed his cousin Mustafa IV on the throne, and he was imprisoned and assassinated in 1808.

[[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] sultan (r. 1512–1520), also known as Selim the Grim or Yavuz Sultan Selim. Despite a reign of only eight years, he greatly expanded the empire. He conquered the [[Mamluk Sultanate]] of Egypt between 1516 and 1517, including the [[Levant]], [[Hejaz]] and Egypt itself. By his death in 1520 the empire spanned about 3.4 million km2 (1.3 million sq mi), having grown by seventy percent during his reign. His conquest of the Middle Eastern heartlands and his role as guardian of the pilgrimage routes to [[Mecca]] and [[Medina]] made the Ottomans the pre-eminent Muslim state. Selim is popularly remembered as the first legitimate Ottoman [[Caliphate|caliph]], although stories of an official transfer of the caliphal office were a later invention.

High medieval Turco-Persian empire of the Qïnïq branch of Oghuz Turks (1037–1308). It was founded in 1037 by Tughril and his brother Chaghri and spanned 3.9 million square kilometers (1.5 million square miles), from [[Anatolia]] and the Levant to the [[Hindu Kush]], and from Central Asia to the Persian Gulf. The Seljuks moved west to conquer [[Baghdad]]. Their victory over the [[Byzantine Empire]] at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071 helped enable the Turkification of Anatolia. The empire played a key role in the [[Crusades|First and Second Crusades]]. A defeat at the Battle of Qatwan in 1141, against the Western Liao dynasty, caused the loss of vast eastern territories and hastened decline. The [[Khwarazmian Empire]] supplanted the Seljuks in the east in 1194, and the [[Sultanate of Rum]], the last surviving Seljuk sultanate, fell in 1308.

Swedish writer and the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1909. Her first novel, *Gösta Berling's Saga*, was published when she was 33, after she submitted its first chapters to a literary contest in the magazine *Idun*. She taught at a girls' high school in Landskrona from 1885 to 1895, then devoted herself to writing. A 1900 visit to the American Colony in [[Jerusalem]] inspired her book *Jerusalem*, and critics compared her to [[Homer]]. In 1914 she became the first woman granted membership of the Swedish Academy. With her Nobel Prize money she bought back her father's Mårbacka estate, where she lived for the rest of her life.

Study of meaning in language. Semantics examines what linguistic meaning is and how words and complex expressions acquire it. It distinguishes sense, the ideas and concepts associated with an expression, from reference, the object to which it points. It contrasts with [[Syntax]], which studies the rules for grammatical sentences, and with [[Pragmatics]], which investigates how people use language. Lexical semantics studies word meaning, phrasal semantics studies how sentences build meaning from their parts, and formal semantics relies on [[Logic|logic]] and mathematics. Together with syntactics and pragmatics, semantics is part of [[Semiotics]]. Its study began in antiquity, but it was not recognized as an independent field until the 19th century.

Capital and largest city of Central Java province, [[Indonesia]] (pop., 2020: 1,653,524). It was a major port during the Dutch colonial era and remains an important regional center and port. Its history goes back to the 9th century, when it was known as Bergota. In 1678 Sunan Amangkurat II promised control of Semarang to the [[Dutch East India Company]] as part of a debt payment, and by 1705 it had officially become a VOC city. The VOC and the later [[Dutch East Indies]] government established [[Tobacco|tobacco]] plantations there and built roads and railroads. In 2020–2022 the ASEAN Clean Tourist City Standard named Semarang the cleanest tourist destination in Southeast Asia. It was Indonesia's ninth most populous city at the 2020 census.

Reproductive biofluid of male or hermaphroditic animals, also called seminal fluid. In humans and placental mammals it is ejaculated through the [[Penis|penis]] via the [[Urethra|urethra]] and carries [[Sperm|spermatozoa]] from the male gonads. Its enzymes and [[Fructose|fructose]] promote sperm survival and help them move from the [[Vagina|vagina]] into the [[Uterus|uterus]]. The seminal vesicles produce about 70% of human semen, while the prostate contributes proteolytic enzymes and citric acid. Basic amines such as spermine and spermidine help buffer the acidic vaginal environment and protect sperm DNA. A 1992 [[World Health Organization]] report described normal human semen as having a volume of 2 mL or greater and a pH of 7.2 to 8.0.

Electronic component that relies on the electronic properties of [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] materials such as silicon or germanium. Its conductivity lies between those of conductors and insulators, and such devices have replaced [[Vacuum tube|vacuum tubes]] in most applications. Doping with impurities such as phosphorus or [[Boron|boron]] creates n-type or p-type material, and a junction between the two forms the basis of the [[Diode|diode]]. As of 2013, billions of [[MOSFET|MOS transistors]] were manufactured every day, making it the most common semiconductor device. Devices are made as discrete components or as [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuits]] containing from hundreds to billions of devices on a single wafer.

Study of signs and of how meaning is created and communicated through them. It is usually divided into syntactics, which addresses how signs are organized; [[Semantics]], which addresses the relation between signs and their meanings; and [[Pragmatics]], which addresses the relation between signs and their users. Signs can be sounds, images, written marks or gestures, and they include icons, which resemble their referents; indexical signs, which have a direct physical link such as smoke signaling fire; and conventional symbols, such as most words. [[Ferdinand de Saussure]] and [[Charles Sanders Peirce]] established semiotics as an independent field in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Because it is interdisciplinary, it has been applied to literature, art and media, as well as to biosemiotics, which examines sign processes in animals and plants.

Branch of the Afroasiatic language family, spoken by more than 460 million people across West Asia, North Africa, the Horn of Africa, Malta and immigrant communities abroad. It includes [[Arabic]], the most widely spoken Semitic language with 411 million native speakers of all varieties, as well as [[Amharic]], Hebrew, [[Aramaic]] and Maltese. Maltese is the only Semitic language written in the [[Latin script]] and the only one that is an official language of the [[European Union]]. The name, first used in the 1780s by the Göttingen school of history, derives from Shem, one of the sons of Noah in the [[Book of Genesis]]. Semitic words are usually built from three-consonant roots, such as k-t-b for "write" in Arabic, with vowels filling in between. Akkadian and Eblaite texts appear from c. 2600 BCE in [[Mesopotamia]].
